strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: existing AV-LLMs use monaural audio and RGB-only inputs, leaving 3D spatial grounding unaddressed; the paper positions itself well against related fragmented efforts (Hear You Are, SAVVY, BAT, N3D-VLM).

The Neural IV is a sensible and physically-grounded contribution: generalizing the acoustic intensity vector (element-wise product of omnidirectional and directional channel features) to a learned latent space is a clean idea, and the cross-evaluation matrix (Table 3) showing better cross-scenario generalization than Classical IV is a convincing ablation.

SpatialSceneQA is a well-engineered benchmark with careful design choices: scene-based train/val/test splits, LibriSpeech speaker-disjoint splits, held-out speaker geometries, visibility constraints, and non-degenerate source-receiver sampling; the appendix documents asset diversity and coordinate conventions.
Comprehensive component ablations (Tables 3-5) that dissect the contributions of the audio encoder, depth encoding, and FOA to both perception and reasoning tasks.
The paper is clearly written, with a well-organized simulation pipeline, explicit metric definitions, and honest reporting of both mean and median errors in some tables.
weaknesses: Central claim is under-supported: the paper repeatedly asserts that 2D-centric AV-LLMs 'fail even after fine-tuning' on joint reasoning, but Table 2 only reports zero-shot results for Qwen2.5-Omni; no fine-tuned monaural/RGB baseline numbers are presented anywhere, so this motivating claim is not evidenced by the experiments shown.

The joint reasoning tasks (D/E) appear to reduce to audio-only DoA estimation followed by simple geometric matching: removing the FOA encoder collapses accuracy to ~43-47% (near random) while removing depth costs only ~4 points. This suggests the tasks do not genuinely probe integrated audio-visual fusion, weakening the 'joint grounding and reasoning' framing and the significance of the reported 99.2-99.5% accuracy.

Near-ceiling performance (99.2-99.5%) on the headline reasoning tasks indicates the benchmark is likely too easy or contains shortcut structure (e.g., gender-labeled target specification, small discrete candidate sets of 2-3 loudspeakers, fixed 1-4m source distances in the same room), raising questions about what the 61k samples actually measure.

Entirely synthetic evaluation: all results come from SoundSpaces 2.0/Habitat-Sim with a single class of inserted loudspeakers and LibriSpeech speech. No real-world or cross-simulator transfer is reported, yet the abstract claims broad advances for 'AI in physical environments.' The claimed 'first spatial audio-visual benchmark with degree-level supervision' also needs qualification given prior simulation-based efforts.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: in Table 5, 'Ours (Classical) w/o Depth' (99.2/98.7) matches or exceeds the full model, contradicting the text's claim that depth encoding is critical; Table 2 reports median visual offset 0.16m while Table 4 reports mean 0.22m/median 0.16m without clarification; the text claims 99.2% on joint reasoning while Table 2 shows 99.5/99.2.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair: BAT is trained with FOA-to-binaural conversion via a default HRTF, and N3D-VLM/Qwen3-VL are evaluated zero-shot on a domain they were not trained for; a stronger evaluation would fine-tune these baselines on the training split, as was done for BAT.
Ablation gains for depth encoding are modest (3D IoU 0.29 to 0.32), and the absolute 3D IoU of 0.32 is low; a mono-RGB baseline fine-tuned on the data is missing to substantiate the necessity claim.

No limitations section and a boilerplate impact statement; no error bars, significance tests, or variance across seeds; code, checkpoints, and data are only promised 'upon acceptance', limiting current reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing AV-LLMs operate on RGB + monaural audio, and a unified end-to-end framework combining RGB-D with FOA spatial audio for 3D grounding is a sensible and reasonably novel direction (Section 2.3 positions it well against Hear You Are and SAVVY).

The SpatialSceneQA dataset construction is carefully engineered: synchronized RGB-D/FOA rendering via SoundSpaces 2.0 and Habitat-Sim, scene-level train/val/test splits, held-out speaker assets (96/12/12 from Hunyuan3D) to test generalization, and visibility constraints to filter degenerate cases (Section 3.1).

The ablation suite is reasonably thorough: cross-evaluation matrices for Classical vs. Neural IV (Table 3), depth-encoding ablations with mean and median statistics (Table 4), and component analysis showing the FOA encoder is indispensable for reasoning (Table 5).
The paper is clearly written, the task taxonomy (Table 1) is well defined, and coordinate-system conventions are documented in the appendix.

The finding that removing the FOA encoder collapses reasoning accuracy to near-random levels (~43-47%) is an informative empirical result about the insufficiency of monaural representations for spatial disambiguation.
weaknesses: A central claim-evidence mismatch: Section 5.2 asserts that mainstream 2D AV-LLMs 'fail even after fine-tuning' on joint reasoning, yet Table 2 only reports Qwen2.5-Omni in a zero-shot setting. No fine-tuned 2D AV-LLM baseline is presented, so the headline claim that explicit 3D modeling is *necessary* is not directly supported by a controlled comparison where the 2D baseline is given the same training data.

The reasoning tasks (D-E) may be substantially easier than framed. Only inserted loudspeakers can emit sound, each is guaranteed at least 500 visible pixels, and answers are 3-way choices (Left/Center/Right). The random baseline is reported as 45.6/47.4 rather than the expected ~33% for 3-way classification, which suggests answer-distribution skew or an ill-calibrated chance level; the w/o-FOA results of 43.8% (above 3-way chance) reinforce this concern. Performance near 99% may partly reflect shortcut cues (e.g., positional priors, gender classification in the audio stream, or simply locating visible loudspeakers visually) rather than deep spatial reasoning.

All experiments are in simulation (SoundSpaces 2.0 + HM3D + LibriSpeech). Despite the framing around 'physical environments,' there is no real-world evaluation or sim-to-real transfer experiment, which limits the significance of the claims about robust DoA under reverberation and overlapping sources.

The Neural IV contribution is incremental: it replaces STFT-based intensity features with a CNN backbone and a Hadamard product in latent space (Eqs. 4-6). Improvements over Classical IV (2.95°→2.21° single-source; 16.09°→13.13° overlap) are meaningful but modest, and the method is close to prior intensity-vector injections into audio LLMs (Tang et al., 2024).

The BAT comparison may be unfairly disadvantaged: FOA data is converted to binaural audio via a default HRTF before feeding BAT, a lossy transformation, rather than adapting BAT's spatial encoder to FOA directly. The claimed superiority on overlap DoA (13.13° vs. 19.09°) is thus confounded.

Table 5 contains an unexplained anomaly: for Classical IV, removing depth encoding slightly improves 2-speaker accuracy (98.6%→98.7%) while the paper claims depth 'assists in spatially distinguishing potential target speakers.' This inconsistency is not discussed.

Evaluation reporting is inconsistent and statistically thin: the main table (Table 2) reports only median angular error, ablations switch to mean values (Table 4), no standard deviations, multiple seeds, or significance tests are provided anywhere, and 3D IoU of 0.32 is modest without distributional context.

Potential leakage/shortcut concerns in the benchmark design are not analyzed: since loudspeakers are the only sound-emitting objects and source positions are sampled within 1-4 m of the receiver, a model with strong depth/visual grounding could narrow candidates considerably without true audio-visual fusion; a vision-only or depth-only upper-bound baseline is missing.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code, checkpoints, and data are only promised 'upon acceptance,' and several key details (overlap SNR/level balancing, number of overlap configurations, how multi-choice options are ordered) are unspecified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing AV-LLMs handle only RGB + monaural audio, and a unified, end-to-end framework combining RGB-D visual grounding with multi-channel FOA spatial audio is a meaningful step beyond modular pipelines like SAVVY and single-source setups like Hear You Are.

Neural IV is a clean, physically motivated idea: generalizing the acoustic intensity vector (element-wise product of omnidirectional and directional channels) into a learnable CNN latent space. The cross-evaluation matrix (Table 3) showing better cross-scenario stability than Classical IV is a well-designed experiment that directly supports the robustness claim.

SpatialSceneQA (61k samples) with degree-level azimuth/elevation supervision, metric 3D boxes, and synchronized FOA is a substantial dataset contribution, with sensible leakage controls (LibriSpeech and HM3D scene splits, held-out synthetic loudspeaker assets).

The component ablations (Tables 4-5) are informative, particularly the collapse to near-random accuracy (~43-47%) when the FOA encoder is removed, which concretely demonstrates that monaural representations cannot solve the spatial disambiguation tasks.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with clearly defined tasks, coordinate conventions (Appendix B), metrics, and training details that support reasonable reproducibility.
weaknesses: A central claim is not supported by the evidence presented: the analysis states that 'mainstream 2D AV-LLMs... fail even after fine-tuning to reliably associate visual objects with acoustic sources,' yet Table 2 reports Qwen2.5-Omni only in a zero-shot setting. No fine-tuned 2D baseline results are shown anywhere in the paper, so the claimed necessity of explicit 3D modeling versus simply fine-tuning the 2D model on this data is not established.

Visual grounding baselines (N3D-VLM, Qwen3-VL) are evaluated zero-shot and score ~0.00-0.01 IoU, which is a weak comparison; N3D-VLM fine-tuned on the task would be the meaningful reference. As presented, the 3D IoU of 0.32 is compared against near-degenerate baselines, and 0.32 IoU / 0.22m mean offset is itself modest relative to the 'strong competitive performance' framing.

The reasoning tasks appear close to saturation (99.2-99.5%), raising concerns about task difficulty and headroom. The random baseline (45.6/47.4) does not match any obvious chance level for the described multi-choice format, and the paper does not explain how answer options are constructed; the tasks may be solvable via a simple audio-DoA-to-nearest-box procedure rather than deeper reasoning.

Table 5 contains an unexplained anomaly: removing depth encoding improves 2-speaker accuracy for the Classical IV variant (98.6 to 98.7) while severely degrading the Neural IV variant (99.2 to 94.9). This inconsistency is not discussed and complicates the interpretation of the depth-encoding ablation.

Everything is fully synthetic (SoundSpaces 2.0, HM3D renders, Hunyuan3D-generated loudspeakers, fixed SoundSpaces HRTF for the BAT baseline). There is no real-world evaluation or sim-to-real analysis, so generalization of both the framework and the Neural IV representation beyond simulation remains unknown. The claim of 'first spatial audio-visual benchmark' also needs qualification given SAVVY and STARSS23.

BAT is evaluated on FOA converted to binaural with a single default HRTF; this conversion choice may disadvantage the baseline in the overlap setting, and the paper does not discuss this potential unfairness.

The Neural IV contribution, while sensible, is incremental (replacing a fixed STFT front-end with a learnable 1D-CNN and MLP); a comparison against other learnable spatial front-ends (e.g., learnable STFT or SALMONN-style spatial encoders) is absent.

There is no limitations section, and some details relevant to rigor are missing (e.g., how azimuth/elevation MAE is aggregated, statistics beyond the median, sample counts per evaluation split). Minor writing issues (e.g., 'appearence', inconsistent naming 'JAEGER-3D') and a placeholder-quality impact statement further reduce polish.
Reproducibility is contingent on a post-acceptance release; no code, data, or checkpoints are currently available.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending AV-LLMs from 2D (RGB + monaural) perception to joint 3D audio-visual grounding via RGB-D and 4-channel FOA is a meaningful step, and the paper convincingly shows the modality gap (Qwen2.5-Omni near random on reasoning; reasoning collapses to ~43-47% when the FOA encoder is removed).

The Neural IV is a sensible, physically-grounded extension of the classical intensity vector: replacing STFT with a learnable data2vec-style CNN frontend and computing latent-space cross-channel interactions yields consistent gains (2.21° vs 2.95° single-source; 4.11° vs 6.44° overlap) and better cross-scenario generalization (Table 3 cross-evaluation matrix).

SpatialSceneQA is a useful, carefully constructed benchmark: synchronized RGB-D + FOA + 3D annotations, scene-level and asset-level (96/12/12 loudspeaker) splits, LibriSpeech speaker splits to avoid leakage, and visibility filtering. It is, to the authors' knowledge, the first benchmark with degree-level azimuth/elevation supervision plus 3D grounding under source overlap.

Evaluation goes beyond the usual headline numbers: the appendix includes a matched-input SimpleFuse ablation (showing gains come from the architecture, not just richer inputs), an FOA-vs-binaural comparison under a matched setup (Table 8), a harder multi-candidate setting that honestly contextualizes the near-ceiling 99% reasoning accuracy (drops to 72.5-80% with 6 candidates), and a small-scale STARSS23 transfer sanity check.

The Impact Statement and Appendix A are candid about limitations: simulation-only evaluation, azimuth transfer to real acoustics remaining difficult (74-77° error), and no claim that sim-to-real is solved.
weaknesses: All main results are simulation-only. The STARSS23 transfer is explicitly a sanity check on 753 single-speaker clips, and even there azimuth median error is ~74° even with pretraining, so real-world applicability of the central claims remains unvalidated. The practical value of the system hinges on this unresolved transfer question.

The main reasoning benchmark (Tasks D/E) appears too easy: accuracy is 98.6-99.5% with only 2-3 candidates, and the harder 4-6 candidate setting is trained with only 160 samples, making it a weak generalization probe rather than a properly calibrated benchmark. The claim of 'multi-step spatial reasoning' is supported mainly by this thin evidence.

3D grounding results are unremarkable and under-analyzed: 3D IoU of 0.32 is modest, and while Table 4 shows depth encoding helps, there is little analysis of failure modes, nor any fine-tuned comparison against N3D-VLM (only zero-shot), making the visual-grounding contribution harder to judge.

Neural IV, while effective, is an incremental design (CNN frontend replacing STFT plus element-wise channel interaction and an MLP); a deeper analysis of why it is more robust to reverberation/overlap (e.g., probing learned features, frequency analysis) would strengthen the contribution beyond empirical gains.

The manuscript states 'source code, pre-trained model checkpoints, and datasets are available at' but the URL is missing, weakening the reproducibility claim at submission time. Comparison with closely related systems (SAVVY, Hear You Are) is limited to discussion rather than empirical evaluation, even if the modality setups differ.
Some evidence of rushed writing (e.g., 'appearence' typo, 'comprehensive ablation studies' grammar, truncated abstract link), suggesting the paper would benefit from another polish pass.

strengths: The integration of RGB-D geometry with 4-channel FOA spatial audio in a single end-to-end AV-LLM is a sensible and reasonably novel direction; most prior work (Hear You Are, SAVVY) either uses RGB-only visuals or a cascaded signal-processing pipeline, so a unified learned approach fills a real gap.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: beyond the main table, the paper includes a cross-evaluation matrix (Table 3), matched-input ablation with SimpleFuse (Table 7) that controls for modality richness, a binaural-vs-FOA comparison under a matched setup (Table 8), a harder multi-candidate reasoning setting (Table 9), depth-encoding and FOA-encoder ablations (Tables 4-5), and a small-scale real-data transfer check on STARSS23 (Table 6).

The Neural IV generalizes the physical intensity-vector computation (element-wise product of omni and directional channels) into a learnable CNN latent space, which is simple, physically motivated, and demonstrably improves robustness under source overlap (4.11° vs 6.44° for Classical IV) and cross-scenario generalization (14.91°/14.85° vs 18.35°/19.25°).

The SpatialSceneQA pipeline is carefully constructed: scene-based train/test splits over HM3D, LibriSpeech split discipline to prevent speaker leakage, unseen loudspeaker meshes for testing, geodesic/Euclidean connectivity constraints for sampling, and visibility filters for grounding targets.

The paper is honest about limitations: the appendix STARSS23 experiment is explicitly framed as a sanity check, the harder-split results explicitly contextualize the near-ceiling main benchmark accuracy, and the Impact Statement discusses sim-to-real transfer and privacy risks of localization capabilities.

Reproducibility appears strong: source code, checkpoints, and the dataset are stated to be released, and training/optimization details (LoRA rank, GPU counts, batch sizes, learning-rate schedule) are provided.
weaknesses: All headline results are simulation-only, and the real-world transfer check is weak: on STARSS23, pretrained Neural IV still achieves a 76.7° median azimuth error (versus 94.9° from scratch), which is close to uninformative for a variable defined on [-180°, 180°]. The paper acknowledges this, but it substantially weakens the claim that explicit 3D modeling enables 'AI in physical environments' beyond the simulator.

The near-ceiling reasoning accuracies (99.5%/99.2%) on the main benchmark indicate the tasks as constructed are too easy, likely solvable by coarse azimuth discrimination plus 2-3 candidates. The appendix harder split (72.5% at 6 candidates, and only 160 training samples per setting) confirms the ceiling is an artifact of benchmark design rather than robust spatial reasoning ability.

The visual grounding baselines are evaluated zero-shot (N3D-VLM, Qwen3-VL obtain 0.00-0.01 IoU), which mostly measures out-of-distribution failure rather than grounding capability; fine-tuning these baselines on Task C would be needed to attribute the gap to JAEGER's design. The absolute 3D IoU of 0.32 is also modest and left uncontextualized.

There is an internal inconsistency: the text states 2D AV-LLMs 'fail even after fine-tuning' on reasoning tasks, but Table 2 reports Qwen2.5-Omni only zero-shot; no fine-tuned monaural baseline on Tasks D-E is actually presented, so the central claim that monaural representations are 'fundamentally insufficient' is under-supported (the SimpleFuse ablation partially addresses this but uses a different, weaker fusion rather than a tuned strong baseline).

The dataset statistics do not reconcile: Table 1 lists 32K + 30K samples for Tasks A-B alone (62K) before Task C's 17+34+9=60K and Tasks D-E's 14K+29K, yet the dataset is described as 61k total. The relationship between #Samples and unique scenes/instances is not explained.

The 'joint' framing is muddied by the training procedure: different component subsets are selectively fine-tuned for different tasks (audio encoder for DoA, visual encoder for grounding, everything for reasoning), leaving unclear whether a single unified JAEGER model performs all tasks or per-task specialist variants.

The Neural IV contribution is technically modest — a 1D-CNN replacing STFT plus a Hadamard product in latent space — and its gains over Classical IV are meaningful only in overlap/cross-scenario settings, with identical 1-speaker reasoning accuracy (99.5% vs 99.5%).

Targeting reasoning queries by LibriSpeech gender labels (Task E) is a coarse and potentially bias-carrying proxy, and no error analysis (e.g., confusion by azimuth sector, failure modes under heavy reverberation) is provided beyond aggregate metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing AV-LLMs are 2D-centric (RGB + monaural), and the proposed JAEGER jointly integrates RGB-D geometry with 4-channel FOA audio in an end-to-end learned framework, rather than a cascaded signal-processing pipeline (contrast with SAVVY).

SpatialSceneQA is a substantial resource contribution: 61k synchronized RGB-D + FOA samples with degree-level DoA, 3D bounding-box, and multi-speaker matching annotations, built on SoundSpaces 2.0 / HM3D with careful leakage controls (LibriSpeech splits, scene-based HM3D partitioning, held-out loudspeaker meshes 96/12/12).

The Neural IV is a clean, physically motivated idea: generalizing the acoustic intensity principle (element-wise interaction between omnidirectional and directional channel features) into a latent space, replacing fixed STFT processing with a learnable CNN. The cross-evaluation matrix (Table 3) convincingly shows better generalization than Classical IV across matched/mismatched source scenarios.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area. The appendix adds matched-input architectural ablation (SimpleFuse, Table 7), FOA vs. binaural comparison under a matched setup (Table 8), a harder multi-candidate reasoning split (Table 9), and a sim-to-real sanity check on STARSS23 (Table 6), which substantially strengthens the empirical case.

The paper is honest about limitations: the impact statement explicitly flags simulation-only evaluation and transfer risk; the harder-split experiment properly contextualizes the near-ceiling 99%+ reasoning accuracies; the STARSS23 experiment is framed as a sanity check rather than full sim-to-real validation.
weaknesses: All quantitative claims rest on a self-constructed simulated benchmark. Real-world transfer is only a small-scale sanity check, and the transfer results are weak: median azimuth error on STARSS23 remains 76.7° even after pretraining (Table 6), which raises questions about whether the learned FOA spatial cues are genuinely robust or substantially simulator-bound.

The headline reasoning results (99.5%/99.2%) are near-ceiling on a benchmark the authors designed themselves, which limits their evidential value; the 2-3 candidate settings appear relatively easy, and the harder split (72.5-95.0% with 4-6 candidates, trained on only 160 samples) suggests the main results overstate capability in realistic distractor-rich scenes.

Baseline comparisons are not fully matched: Qwen2.5-Omni is evaluated zero-shot and is declared 'inherently incapable' of DoA; N3D-VLM and Qwen3-VL are zero-shot for grounding; BAT is retrained on converted binaural audio. The SimpleFuse ablation partially mitigates this, but there is still no fine-tuned, equal-compute baseline adapting a modern omni model to the tasks, making the 'fundamental modality gap' claim harder to verify cleanly.

Novelty of the technical core is moderate: 3D-aware positional encoding from depth is adapted from prior work (Zheng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), the dual-path audio design follows Tang et al. (2024), and Neural IV is an incremental learnable replacement for STFT-based features; the main novelty weight rests on the joint framework and dataset.

Some reported numbers are modest and under-analyzed: a 3D IoU of 0.32 for grounding is usable but far from precise; the paper does not report variance across seeds, error distributions beyond median, or statistical significance for the Neural vs. Classical IV differences (e.g., 99.2% vs. 98.6%).

The reasoning tasks (D-E) risk shallow shortcuts (e.g., coarse left/center/right discrimination), and the paper does not probe whether the model performs genuine metric DoA-to-geometry alignment versus exploiting position-encoding correlations; finer-grained analyses of failure modes would strengthen the 'multi-step spatial reasoning' claim.
